title: What If a Year Lasted 445 Days? Rome's Did in 46 BC

scenes.text: What if one year had 445 days? Rome lived through it, and called it the year of confusion.
The old Roman calendar had 355 days, with extra days added now and then. The seasons drifted.
By 50 BC the spring equinox was falling in mid-May, about eight weeks late.
Julius Caesar called in the astronomer Sosigenes. To reset the seasons, 46 BC got its usual 23 extra days, plus two extra months: 67 more.
Four hundred and forty-five days in one year. Then, from 45 BC, a 365-day year with a leap day every fourth year.
That calendar ran for over 1,600 years, and is one small fix from the one on your phone. The price: one very long year.

description:
What if a single year lasted 445 days? In 46 BC it did: Julius Caesar, advised by the astronomer Sosigenes of Alexandria, added two extra months (67 days) on top of the usual 23-day insertion to pull the drifting Roman calendar back in line with the seasons.
The spring equinox had slipped about eight weeks late; from 45 BC Rome used a 365-day year with a leap day every fourth year, the Julian calendar that the Gregorian reform later fine-tuned.
